title: 2D Sperner's Lemma and PPAD Complexity Connection
description: Formalizes 2D Sperner's lemma on a standard grid triangulation via door-counting. Proves the number of fully-colored triangles is odd. Connects to Brouwer OQ-02 (PPAD complexity): Chen-Deng (2009) showed finding a fully-colored simplex in a Sperner triangulation is PPAD-complete. 20 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Chen-Deng (2009) proved that finding a fully-colored simplex in a 2D Sperner triangulation is PPAD-complete. This is the combinatorial backbone of Brouwer fixed-point hardness results.
overview.problemStatement: Prove the 2D Sperner's lemma: on a grid triangulation of the unit triangle with a valid Sperner coloring, the number of fully-colored triangles is odd (≥ 1).
overview.proofStrategy: Door-counting: (1) each fully-colored triangle has exactly 1 door (edge colored {0,1}). (2) Each non-fully-colored triangle has 0 or 2 doors. (3) Boundary {0,1} doors are odd (1D Sperner on bottom edge). (4) Interior doors pair up. Therefore #(fully-colored triangles) is odd.
keyInsights: **Door-counting parity**: count edges colored {0,1} (doors). Each fully-colored triangle contributes 1 door; the parity of fully-colored triangles equals the parity of boundary doors.
**1D Sperner boundary**: the bottom edge of the grid gives a 1D Sperner instance — a walk from 0 to 1 must have an odd number of {0,1} crossings.
**PPAD connection**: PPAD (Polynomial Parity Arguments on Directed graphs) captures search problems whose solution existence follows from a parity argument — exactly Sperner's structure.

sections.title: 2D Grid Sperner via Door-Counting
sections.summary: Grid triangulation definitions, Sperner coloring constraints, door-counting lemmas, parity argument. Main result: odd #fully-colored triangles.

conclusion.summary: 20 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. 2D Sperner's lemma proved via door-counting. PPAD connection documented.
conclusion.implications: The 2D Sperner lemma is the foundation for Chen-Deng PPAD-completeness of Brouwer fixed-point computation. This formalization supports the connection between combinatorics and computational complexity.
openQuestions: Can the n-dimensional Sperner's lemma be proved by the same door-counting technique?
Can the PPAD-completeness reduction from 2D Sperner to Brouwer be formalized?
Can the Kakutani fixed-point theorem be derived from the 2D Sperner lemma?
